w8-formal~idea.cta: The formal word on the Word road
w8-formal~idea.title: The formal word
w8-formal~idea.body: Many everyday words have a formal partner with the same meaning. In a letter to someone you do not know, a report or a notice, the formal word sounds respectful and clear: "inform" for "tell", "error" for "mistake". With friends, the everyday word is the right one. Register is choosing on purpose.
w8-formal~idea.more: I can swap an everyday word for a formal one.

s8-spot~idea.cta: Spot the odd one out on the Sentence road
s8-spot~idea.title: Spot the odd one out
s8-spot~idea.body: Parts that do the same job in a sentence should have the same shape: reading, writing and swimming — not reading, writing and to swim. Great speeches and books use matching shapes on purpose, so the ideas line up in the listener's mind.
s8-spot~idea.more: I can spot the part of a sentence that breaks its pattern.

s8-fix~idea.cta: Make it match on the Sentence road
s8-fix~idea.title: Make it match
s8-fix~idea.body: To fix a sentence that is not parallel, find the pattern most of its parts already follow, then rebuild the odd part in the same shape: a verb to match verbs, an adjective to match adjectives, "to" to match "to". Pairs joined by than, or, either…or and not only…but also must match too.
s8-fix~idea.more: I can rebuild a sentence so its matching parts match.

li8-periods~idea.cta: The ages of writing on the Literature road
li8-periods~idea.title: The ages of writing
li8-periods~idea.body: Writers belong to their times. The Elizabethan age (the late 1500s, Shakespeare's time) loved plays and sonnets. The 18th century brought the first English novels, such as Robinson Crusoe and Gulliver's Travels. The Romantic poets (about 1790 to 1830) wrote about nature and feeling. The Victorian age (1837 to 1901) was the age of the great novel: Dickens, the Brontës, Alice. Edwardian writers (from 1901) gave us The Wind in the Willows and Peter Rabbit.
li8-periods~idea.more: I can place a work in its age.

la8-modifiers~idea.cta: Who is doing it? on the Language road
la8-modifiers~idea.title: Who is doing it?
la8-modifiers~idea.body: An opening phrase such as "Running for the bus" describes whoever comes next in the sentence. If the next words are "my hat", the hat is running! Fix it by putting the person straight after the phrase: "Running for the bus, I lost my hat." Clear writing also prefers the active voice — "The dog chased the ball", not "The ball was chased by the dog" — so the reader knows who did what.
la8-modifiers~idea.more: I can fix a dangling modifier and choose the active voice.

la8-modifiers~story.cta: Who is doing it? on the Language road
la8-modifiers~story.title: Who is doing it?
la8-modifiers~story.body: Quill reads a note on the fridge: "Running for the bus, my hat blew away." "Was the hat running?" Quill laughs. A sentence can say something its writer never meant.
